processing: A bud with one to two (some accounts say up to three) young leaves is withered at length and then dried at low heat, with no firing or rolling.
harvest_season: Spring, after the first bud-only silver needle picking and before the coarser gong mei and shou mei.
appearance_dry: Downy silver buds among loose olive-green and silvery leaves.
appearance_liquor: Clear pale gold, deeper than silver needle.
appearance_wet: Whole soft sets of bud and leaves in yellow-green, with a pale midrib.
taste_profile: More layered than silver needle: honey, white peach and hay over a soft, slightly creamy body, as commonly described for the grade.

brewing.notes: Leaf gives flavour faster than buds, so steeps can be shorter than for silver needle. Long steeps in very hot water bring out dryness.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, either loose and fresh from the current spring or pressed into cakes and kept for several years with the year stated. Grades vary by how many buds are in the mix, and stored lots shift from floral towards honey and hay.
description:
White Peony from Fuding is the bud-and-leaf grade that sits between silver needle and the coarser shou mei. The source plants are generally the same big-white cultivars, and it is the leaves that make the difference: they add flavour that a bud alone cannot.

It is made the same simple way as other whites, by a long wither and then gentle drying with no rolling. Slight oxidation in withering takes off raw green notes and leaves a softer, more floral leaf. Because the leaves are less protected than down-covered buds, the wither shows clearly in the cup.

Descriptions usually run to honey, white peach and hay, with a soft body. Across steeps it starts floral and turns sweeter. Treat these notes as a guide, since batches vary a lot and much of the language comes from sellers.

Look for whole sets of bud and leaf with visible down, and little that is dark or broken. A cake is convenient for keeping, but loose leaf lets you see what you are buying.
history: Bai mu dan belongs to the Fujian tradition of grading white tea by the plant and the picking, in which big-white or Shui Xian shoots of a bud and two or three leaves make the grade. Modern white tea craft developed in Qing dynasty Fuding, and it was exported from the Guangxu years, with peak trade in the early Republic. A separate dated history for the Fuding version of this grade is little documented.
